stories.headline: U.S. envoys head to Kyiv after long Kremlin meeting
stories.dek: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Kyiv after three hours of closed-door talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
paragraphs: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due in Kyiv on Sunday after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow the day before. Washington is trying to restart peace talks on Russia's invasion of Ukraine after months in which U.S. attention shifted to the Iran war.

The Moscow meeting lasted more than three hours and ended without any public deal. Russian aide Yuri Ushakov called the talks constructive and said they covered both the war and possible U.S.-Russia economic projects. Witkoff and Kushner last visited Moscow in January for another round of Kremlin talks.

The fighting has not paused in any broad sense. Russia and Ukraine traded overnight drone and missile attacks despite an understanding to avoid strikes on each other's capitals during talks. It is still unclear whether the Kyiv visit will produce a ceasefire proposal, direct negotiations, or only another round of shuttle diplomacy.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means U.S. diplomacy on Ukraine is active again and new proposals could emerge soon.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean a ceasefire is in place or that the war's front lines are about to change quickly.

cover.title: U.S. envoys travel to Kyiv after meeting Putin in Moscow
cover.standfirst: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due in Kyiv on Sunday after more than three hours of closed-door talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow. No breakthrough was announced, and Russia and Ukraine still exchanged overnight drone and missile attacks as the U.S. tries to revive stalled peace talks.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: Show a passenger jet descending diagonally from upper left toward Kyiv, but make only its nose and cockpit transform into unmistakable Saint Basil-style onion domes. Print the aircraft as a flat black silhouette and overprint the domes in slightly misregistered red so the front of the plane feels infected by Moscow; keep Kyiv as a low, dark skyline pushed to the top edge, with the entire lower third left open and quiet for type. Strip out all other detail: no clouds, no windows, no extra city texture — just the arrival vector and the contamination.
art.note: Tense and restrained; deep blue, black, and muted red.
art.second_beat: First read: envoys flying to Kyiv; second beat: the trip itself arrives carrying the Kremlin inside it.

stories.headline: US says it destroyed three Iranian oil tankers
stories.dek: Washington said the strikes answered recent attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway vital to global oil trade.
paragraphs: The US military said it destroyed three Iranian oil tankers after attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz. The statement presents the action as retaliation and a warning against further disruption in one of the world's most important shipping lanes. The strikes were announced about an hour ago.

The Strait of Hormuz sits between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula. A large share of the world's oil passes through it by sea. Any attack on ships there can raise fears over energy supply, insurance costs and wider fighting between the United States, Iran and their partners.

Key facts are still missing. The US account has not been matched here with Iranian confirmation, casualty details or evidence on the earlier ship attacks. It is also unclear where the tankers were hit, whether crews were evacuated, and how Iran or other naval forces in the region will respond.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this raises the risk of higher oil and shipping costs if the waterway becomes less safe.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean oil supplies have stopped or that a wider war is certain today.

cover.title: US says it destroyed three Iranian oil tankers
cover.standfirst: The US military said it struck three Iranian oil tankers after attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz. The narrow passage carries a large share of global oil by sea. Casualties, the exact strike locations and Iran's response were still unclear.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: Make the Strait of Hormuz the whole image: a solid black landmass fills the upper two-thirds, leaving the waterway as a narrow negative channel. At its eastern mouth, from the Gulf of Oman side, that channel becomes unmistakably a lit fuse — just a small red ember and a ragged red-burnt edge eating inward along the strait — while the lower third stays pale and empty for type. No ships, no extra map detail, no labels: only the specific pinch-point geography, simplified enough that the strait itself reads first as a fuse and then as the real route for oil traffic.
art.note: Severe and spare; black, navy, rust red and dull orange.
art.second_beat: First you see a fuse burning toward an explosion; a beat later you realise the fuse is the actual Strait of Hormuz, making the place itself look primed to detonate.

stories.headline: Regulator says Medtronic hid poor results for back pain implant
stories.dek: A confidential Australian review found the company’s own larger patient data showed its spinal implant may offer little real benefit.
paragraphs: Australia’s medical regulator has accused Medtronic of hiding data that showed its Intellis spinal cord stimulator worked far worse than advertised. The allegation is public now because a confidential Therapeutic Goods Administration report was obtained under freedom of information laws and reviewed by reporters.

The Intellis is an implanted device used for chronic back pain. Medtronic promoted it using a 128-person study published in 2021 that said most patients cut pain by more than half. But the regulator said Medtronic’s unpublished real-world data from a larger group showed much weaker results and possible serious risks.

It is still unclear what action regulators will take against Medtronic, how many Australians received the device after the poor data was known, and when officials learned of the results. Questions also remain over approval of Medtronic’s newer Inceptiv stimulator, which relied on claims that it was equivalent to Intellis.
stories.changes: Patients considering implanted pain devices may need to ask for full evidence, not just published trial results or marketing claims.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean every spinal cord stimulator fails or that every patient with an implant should panic or seek urgent removal.

cover.title: Australian regulator says Medtronic hid poor back implant data
cover.standfirst: A confidential Therapeutic Goods Administration report says Medtronic’s own larger patient data showed its Intellis spinal cord stimulator may offer little meaningful benefit for back pain. The implant was approved in Australia in 2018. It is still unclear what penalties or product reviews will follow.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat signal-red ground, show a surgeon’s gloved hand mid-procedure pushing a spinal cord stimulator lead into a stark black-and-white cutout lower spine. The lead is unmistakably not a medical wire but a torn strip of photocopied report paper — pale grey with copier grain, ruled lines, and a ragged perforated edge — snaking into the incision like something being hidden inside the body. Add one crude black marker arrow driving toward the entry point; keep the lower third largely empty for type.
art.note: Cold, accusatory mood; steel blue, off-white, black, with a small warning red accent.
art.second_beat: First you see an implant being inserted; a beat later you realize the implant itself is the buried review data.

stories.headline: Iran attacks keep Strait of Hormuz shipping in deadlock
stories.dek: Fresh attacks and military patrols have left one of the world's busiest oil routes dangerous and hard to reopen.
paragraphs: Iran has kept up attacks around the Strait of Hormuz, sustaining a military stalemate with the United States and Gulf allies. The waterway remains dangerous for merchant ships. That matters now because the strait carries a large share of global oil and gas exports.

The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman. Tankers from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and other producers use it to reach world markets. When traffic is threatened there, shipping costs rise, deliveries slow and energy prices can jump.

No clear path to normal traffic has emerged. Iran is still using pressure in the strait as leverage, while U.S. and allied forces continue patrols and retaliatory actions. Markets and shippers are watching for new talks, fresh attacks or official statements that signal either de-escalation or a wider clash.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this raises the risk of higher fuel and goods prices if shipping disruption lasts.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the strait is fully closed or that a broader regional war is certain.

cover.title: Iran attacks leave Strait of Hormuz shipping in dangerous deadlock
cover.standfirst: Iran's continued attacks have kept the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and gas, in a military standoff with U.S. and Gulf forces. Commercial shipping remains exposed to disruption two hours after the latest report, and no near-term deal to restore normal traffic is in sight.

art.label: Maximalist doodle
art.concept: Fill the upper two-thirds with a dense, almost decorative stream of near-identical side-on crude tankers packed bow-to-stern so their overall mass quietly resolves into the shape of the Strait of Hormuz. At the narrow throat, one single supertanker is swung hard across the channel, visibly jamming the procession, while two or three tiny patrol craft arc around its bow and stern mid-manoeuvre; keep the lower third largely open water with only a few trailing hulls so type can sit cleanly.
art.note: Severe and tense; deep navy, black, rust red.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a patterned tanker convoy; a beat later you see the whole route is being defined and blocked by the one ship turned sideways at Hormuz’s pinch point.

stories.headline: US envoys meet Putin in Moscow for Ukraine war talks
stories.dek: The three-hour Kremlin meeting produced a narrow pause on strikes toward Kyiv, but no wider ceasefire along the front.
paragraphs: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Vladimir Putin in Moscow for more than three hours on Sept. 5 to discuss ways to stop the war in Ukraine. The talks matter now because both sides say they are preparing next diplomatic steps, with the envoys due in Kyiv next.

The Kremlin said the US side brought specific settlement ideas and that the discussion was constructive. Putin also said Russian strikes on Kyiv would pause from midnight, after a request passed through official channels. But he rejected Ukraine’s call for a broader three-day ceasefire across the whole front line.

Nothing close to a peace deal was announced. Fighting continues along the front, and Russia is still repeating its long-standing demands about territory and the causes of the war. It is also unclear whether the limited pause around the two capitals will hold, or whether Kyiv and Moscow can widen it.
stories.changes: For readers, this means there is a live diplomatic channel between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, with possible next steps soon.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the war is near an end, or that Russia has accepted a general ceasefire.

cover.title: US envoys hold three-hour Kremlin meeting with Putin
cover.standfirst: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Sept. 5 for more than three hours to discuss possible terms for ending the war in Ukraine. Putin said strikes on Kyiv would pause, but he refused a wider three-day ceasefire. The envoys are due in Kyiv next.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a pale Kremlin-red seamless set, place a single clear glass ashtray slightly above centre, leaving the lower third completely empty for type. Inside it, a small folded blue-and-yellow road map is caught mid-smoulder: only the exposed top edges are burning, with one blackened corner, a thin curl of ash lifting, and the flame visibly contained by the glass rim. Keep everything else absent and still, so the ashtray reads first as a neat diplomatic object, then as a ceasefire zone absurdly too small for the war.
art.note: Controlled and tense; muted red, black, cream and dull gold.
art.second_beat: The second beat is that the ashtray’s rim becomes the boundary of protection: one tiny area is contained while everything beyond it remains outside the pause.

stories.headline: German rocket reaches orbit from Norway on second flight
stories.dek: Isar Aerospace deployed satellites from Andoya, becoming the first European commercial launcher to reach orbit from European soil.
paragraphs: Isar Aerospace sent its Spectrum rocket into orbit on Saturday night from Andoya in northern Norway and released several small satellites. The German company says this is the first time a commercial European launcher has reached orbit from European soil. The timing matters because European leaders meet in Paris this week to discuss space independence.

Spectrum is a 28-metre rocket built for smaller satellite missions. It can carry about 1,000 kilograms to low Earth orbit. Isar’s first launch, in March last year, failed after about 30 seconds. This mission flew after delays caused by weather, technical problems and a boat entering the launch range.

The harder part starts now. One successful flight does not prove that Isar can launch often, cheaply or on schedule. Its latest payloads were backed by public programmes, not normal commercial customers. Europe already had access to space through Ariane 6 from French Guiana, so the open question is whether private launches from Europe can become routine.
stories.changes: It gives European satellite builders one more possible launch option closer to home.
stories.unchanged: It does not end Europe’s reliance on larger foreign rockets or make space launches cheap overnight.

cover.title: Isar Aerospace reaches orbit from Norway on second launch
cover.standfirst: Isar Aerospace launched its 28-metre Spectrum rocket from Andoya in northern Norway at 22:12 CEST on Saturday and deployed satellites about four minutes later. The flight made it the first commercial European company to reach orbit from European soil. The next test is whether it can do this regularly for paying customers.

art.label: Minimal mark
art.concept: On a vast pale field, place a single tiny black Spectrum silhouette high and slightly off-centre, leaving the entire lower third empty for type. The form begins as a straight vertical rocket, but its upper end cleanly kinks into a thin sideways orbital arc, so one continuous shape shows the exact instant ascent becomes orbit; keep everything else out — no Earth, no stars, no extra satellites, no smoke.
art.note: Clean, stark, night-launch palette with deep blue, black and hot white-orange flame.
art.second_beat: First read: a rocket launch; second beat: the rocket’s own shape has already turned into an orbit, making this specifically the threshold from liftoff in Norway to successful orbital insertion.

stories.headline: Russian attacks kill eight across Ukraine during Kyiv pause
stories.dek: Air defenses downed most of 108 drones, but strikes and falling debris still killed civilians in several regions.
paragraphs: Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured at least 69 across Ukraine over the past day, officials said on Sept. 6. Fires broke out in Kyiv Oblast and Dnipropetrovsk Oblast overnight. The attacks came as U.S. envoys were due in Kyiv for talks, under a declared pause on strikes against capitals.

Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 108 drones overnight. Air defenses intercepted 82 drones and six missiles, but strikes still hit 11 locations and debris fell in seven more. The dead included an 11-year-old boy and a 19-year-old woman in Chuhuiv, in Kharkiv Oblast. Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Donetsk and other regions were also hit.

Officials said there were no reported hits in the city of Kyiv overnight, though the wider region was attacked and alerts sounded. Casualty counts may still rise as rescue work continues. It is also unclear whether the pause on attacks against capitals will hold after the U.S. visit and whether the talks will reduce strikes elsewhere.
stories.changes: For ordinary Ukrainians, the reported pause around Kyiv did not mean a safer night across the country.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean fighting has slowed overall or that a broader ceasefire is close.

cover.title: Russian attacks kill eight across Ukraine despite Kyiv pause
cover.standfirst: Russian strikes killed at least eight people and injured 69 across Ukraine in the past day, even as officials reported no overnight hits inside Kyiv city. Air defenses shot down most of 108 drones, but attacks still caused fires, deaths and evacuations in several regions as U.S. envoys arrived for peace talks.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: Show one ordinary Soviet-era apartment stack in Chuhuiv as a single continuous engraved facade split cleanly down the middle. Left half: intact windows, curtains, and on one small balcony a child’s bicycle; right half: the same flats moments after the night strike, windows blown out, wall broken open, curtains sucked outward, a few shards still dropping through the black. Keep the lower third quiet with dark wall mass and a bare strip of ground; in the ruined half, that same balcony is now empty except for one bicycle wheel hanging over the rail.
art.note: Quiet, severe, smoke-gray and ember-orange palette.
art.second_beat: The image lands first as a blunt before-and-after, then the missing bicycle and lone wheel make the civilian loss arrive a beat later.

stories.headline: US says Iranian tanker sank after strike in Gulf of Oman
stories.dek: US Central Command released video it says shows the tanker M/T Kylo going down after a US attack.
paragraphs: The US military says an Iranian oil tanker sank in the Gulf of Oman after a US strike. US Central Command released video that it says shows the vessel, named M/T Kylo, listing and going under. The footage was published hours after reports of attacks by both the US and Iran on ships.

The Gulf of Oman is a narrow sea route between the Arabian Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, a key path for global oil shipments. Any attack there matters beyond the ships involved. The report says the tanker was Iranian, but public details about its cargo, crew, flag and exact route remain limited.

It is still unclear when exactly the strike happened, whether there were casualties, and what legal basis the US gave for hitting the tanker. Independent verification of the video is also unresolved. Iran's account of the incident, and whether it will answer with further attacks at sea, is not yet clear.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this raises the risk of higher shipping and energy costs if fighting at sea spreads.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean oil supplies have stopped or that civilian shipping through the region has closed.

cover.title: US says Iranian tanker sank after strike in Gulf of Oman
cover.standfirst: US Central Command released video it says shows the tanker M/T Kylo sinking in the Gulf of Oman after a US attack. The waterway is a key route for world oil trade. Casualties, the ship's cargo and Iran's response were still unclear on Saturday.

art.label: Made object
art.concept: Cut the scene to almost nothing: a flat blue sea fills the cover, pinched between two unmistakable coloured-card coastlines shaped as Iran and Oman, so the narrow Gulf of Oman / Hormuz approach is instantly legible as the choke point. In that blue gap, the water itself forms the silhouette of a tanker tipping nose-first under, with the bow disappearing into the lower third and a tiny burst of orange flame and black smoke at the top edge of the ship-shape to signal the strike; keep the bottom third as plain blue water for type.
art.note: Severe and spare; deep navy, black and rust red.
art.second_beat: First you see the strategic map of the Gulf choke point; a beat later you realise the sea lane itself is also the sinking tanker, turning one strike into a story about the whole oil route.

stories.headline: Anak Krakatau eruption suspends hundreds of flights in Indonesia
stories.dek: Ash from the volcano forced widespread flight suspensions as airlines and airports tried to avoid dangerous conditions.
paragraphs: Indonesia's Mount Anak Krakatau has erupted, disrupting air travel and leading to the suspension of hundreds of flights. The immediate problem is volcanic ash, which can damage aircraft engines and reduce visibility. Airlines and airport authorities moved quickly because ash clouds can spread fast after an eruption.

Anak Krakatau sits in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra. It is one of Indonesia's best known active volcanoes and has erupted before. When it sends ash high into the air, flights in the region can be delayed, diverted or cancelled because planes are not meant to fly through dense volcanic ash.

It is not yet clear how long the flight suspensions will last or how large the ash plume will become. Officials will need to track the volcano and nearby airspace before services return to normal. Travelers may face delays, rebooking problems and changing airport schedules while the situation develops.
stories.changes: Air passengers in and around Indonesia may need to check flight status, expect delays and prepare for cancellations.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all air travel in Indonesia has stopped or that the eruption threatens every part of the country.

cover.title: Anak Krakatau eruption halts hundreds of flights in Indonesia
cover.standfirst: Mount Anak Krakatau erupted in Indonesia, sending ash into the air and forcing hundreds of flight suspensions. Airlines and airports acted because volcanic ash can damage aircraft engines. Officials are now tracking the plume to decide when routes can safely reopen.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: Paint a simple map-view of the Sunda Strait and western Indonesia in flat, quiet colour, with Anak Krakatau unmistakably erupting from the strait. The ash plume must do the whole job: its main branches spread across the Java Sea in the exact visual logic of airline route lines, reaching toward the recognisable positions of Jakarta, Lampung and Bali, but remaining clearly dirty, wind-torn ash rather than graphic marks; near one branch, a tiny airliner banks sharply away at the edge of the frame. Keep the lower third mostly calm sea so type can sit there, and strip out any extra airport detail or labels.
art.note: Calm but tense; muted blue sea, grey-black ash, small sharp white aircraft.
art.second_beat: First you read a flight-route map; a beat later you realise the routes are the ash cloud itself, and the plane is fleeing the network.

stories.headline: Voters in Saxony-Anhalt cast ballots in high-stakes state election
stories.dek: The far-right AfD hopes to win an outright majority and lead a German state government for the first time since World War II.
paragraphs: Voters in Saxony-Anhalt went to the polls Sunday in a state election with national weight. The far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD, is trying to win enough seats to govern alone. If it does, Germany would get its first far-right state government of the postwar era.

Saxony-Anhalt is an eastern state of about 2.1 million people. AfD has built strong support in eastern Germany, where incomes are lower and anger at Berlin runs deeper. Other parties say they will not govern with AfD, whose regional branch is classified by domestic intelligence as right-wing extremist.

It is still unclear whether AfD can win an absolute majority in the state legislature. If it falls short, it may finish first but still be shut out of power. Then Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats would face hard coalition talks with smaller parties to keep governing.
stories.changes: This vote could test whether Germany's long-running refusal to work with AfD can still hold at the state level.
stories.unchanged: It does not by itself change Germany's national government, laws, or immigration policy on Monday.

cover.title: Saxony-Anhalt votes in election that could put AfD in power
cover.standfirst: Voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt cast ballots Sunday in an election that could deliver the first far-right state government in postwar Germany. AfD wants an outright majority in the 2.1 million-person state. If it falls short, other parties may still block it from office.

art.label: Newsprint collage
art.concept: A standard German wall socket is staged as the state parliament: unmistakably a domestic Schuko faceplate in newsprint collage, centred in the upper half, with its two round holes reading as the seat of power. From the lower left, a two-pronged plug folded from plain ballot-paper forms is being pushed toward it but held a breath short of contact, with a few tiny torn-white paper sparks in the gap; keep the lower third largely flat painted colour so cover lines can sit cleanly.
art.note: Tense, civic mood; muted cream, dark blue, red, and charcoal.
art.second_beat: First you see votes trying to connect to power; a beat later you get the sting that winning the vote may still leave the AfD shut out of government.
